description: A team of CS students from Korea.
summary:
BioTwin Sync is an offline research prototype for crew health monitoring and delayed medical consultation during deep-space missions. It combines measurement capture, personal history, physiological-signal review and a simulated crew–Earth consultation workflow.

Its central feature is Executable Conditional Protocols: a flight surgeon reviews delivered evidence and writes branching instructions with explicit conditions. In our demonstration, communication takes 20 minutes each way. When instructions arrive, the onboard evaluator checks them against the newest compatible readings and selects the corresponding branch. Missing, stale or unsuitable evidence produces UNKNOWN, prompting further review instead of an unsupported selection. The crew explicitly records completed actions.

Beyond this workflow, separate research tools process real NASA SOTERIA ECG/BVP recordings, run trained random-forest models for experimental ECG signal review, and use NASA WinSCAT records to investigate personal cognitive references. Model evaluations document both successful controlled-corruption detection and failed natural-signal validation.

The current application runs locally on one computer with separate crew and flight-surgeon views. Its onboard assistant uses source-linked rules; experimental models remain manual-review tools. BioTwin demonstrates traceable evidence handling under communication delay, with clinical validation and flight qualification remaining future work.
details:
A crew member’s condition can change while medical advice is travelling from Earth.

In our simulated mission, a message takes 20 minutes to reach Earth and another 20 minutes to return. A flight surgeon reviews the evidence they received and prepares instructions. Meanwhile, the crew records new measurements. By the time the reply arrives, the situation may have changed.

BioTwin Sync addresses this gap between the evidence used to write an instruction and the evidence available when it arrives. It is an offline research prototype that combines crew health monitoring with delayed medical consultation.

We made the instructions conditional on current evidence.

The flight surgeon writes alternative instructions with explicit conditions. When the reply arrives, BioTwin checks those conditions against the newest compatible onboard measurements, including their freshness, recorded quality and timing.

The software selects the applicable branch or returns UNKNOWN with an explanation when the evidence is missing, stale or unsuitable. The human authors the instructions; the software checks their applicability. Crew members explicitly record completed actions.

Our synthetic demonstration makes this behavior visible: Earth reviews a reaction-time reading of 420 milliseconds while a newer onboard reading becomes 585 milliseconds. The evaluator selects the branch corresponding to the newer evidence. When that same reading becomes too old, it returns UNKNOWN. The values and threshold are illustrative workflow fixtures.

Separate crew and flight-surgeon views preserve what each side actually knows. Earth sees delivered evidence, while the crew retains access to current onboard observations.

That solution depends on understanding the evidence behind each measurement.

A recent value is not automatically a comparable or reliable value. We used two complementary NASA datasets to investigate this evidence layer:

NASA SOTERIA: Real ECG and blood-volume-pulse recordings from ground-based commercial-pilot flight simulations. We checked source files against acquisition manifests, parsed samples and timestamps, and prepared attributed excerpts for offline playback and analysis. Original values, source identities, timing and gaps remain traceable. These are terrestrial research recordings.

NASA Life Sciences Portal WinSCAT Campaign 3: We structured 272 cognitive assessments from 26 deidentified participants into 2,448 observations across nine metrics. Participant identity, measurement method, study phase, source file and original time information remain attached to each observation. Missing values and unresolved units or timezones remain explicit.

These datasets support waveform processing, experimental model training and historical-reference research. They remain separate from the synthetic consultation demonstration.

The historical data showed why personal baselines must sometimes be unavailable.

Our personal-reference engine uses only earlier usable observations from the same person under compatible measurement conditions. It excludes the current observation and future records, and requires at least five compatible earlier values.

Only 18 WinSCAT metric observations met that requirement. Although the dataset contained thousands of observations, it rarely supported the personal reference we needed. BioTwin therefore reports insufficient evidence instead of manufacturing a baseline.

Additional research tools implement cumulative-sum change detection and dynamic time warping to compare compatible historical trajectories. These provide descriptive context rather than diagnoses or predictions of astronaut outcomes.

We also investigated when physiological recordings become unsuitable for signal analysis.

The signal-processing backend implements moving-baseline removal, smoothing, peak detection and timing checks for source-specific engineering estimates. Recording tools identify flat segments, clipping and unusual variation, and support annotations and repeat-measurement requests.

We then trained two random-forest models to examine different kinds of ECG disruption. Each uses 24 trees, a maximum depth of five and 12 engineered features from nominal ten-second windows. Participants were separated across training, validation and testing.

Controlled technical corruption: The model detected deliberately injected sample holds, clipping and noise with 98.63% balanced accuracy, compared with 87.82% for fixed rules. This supports its use in the controlled-corruption demonstration; it does not establish general reliability on natural recordings.

Natural recording exclusions: The second model investigated the source researchers’ heartbeat-detector exclusion labels. It achieved 44.16% balanced accuracy, compared with 51.62% for fixed rules, and failed its deployment criterion. We retained this negative result and kept original recordings subject to manual review.

The controlled experiment used 182 original windows and 546 correlated injected variants from two held-out participants. These windows are not independent people. Unmarked recordings are not assumed to be clean, and neither model is used for clinical decision-making.

The unsuccessful experiments also shaped the project’s boundaries.

A separate ECG count-reliability experiment used a logistic error scorer trained on annotated MIT-BIH recordings. It retained 72 of 180 held-out windows, representing 40% coverage. On that selected subset, the mean absolute count-rate error was 0.58 beats per minute. Coverage was uneven across participants, and the overall acceptance criteria failed.

Frozen sampling checks also rejected all 120 selected NASA evaluation windows, revealing an unresolved input-compatibility problem. A four-policy communication experiment completed 384 combinations under matched byte budgets and delays, but unavailable physiological estimates limited the findings to transport behavior. These experiments establish neither clinical accuracy nor bandwidth superiority.

The working prototype brings evidence collection and delayed consultation into an inspectable workflow.

Users can enter measurements, import supported records, perform a five-trial laptop reaction check, inspect personal history and physiological recordings, and export sessions. The onboard assistant supports structured evidence collection, source-linked guidance, recorded actions and reassessment through a versioned rule library. It uses neither a language model nor a trained diagnostic model.

The application runs on one Windows computer, simulating crew and Earth roles. Python supports the backend, while React runs inside Electron and Chromium. Scikit-learn supported model training; exported forest weights run locally using Python’s standard library without a GPU or cloud inference service.

The current React application, separate native Tk research companion and source-only scientific benchmarks are explicitly distinguished in the repository’s judge tour. Snapshot fingerprints and version checks support consistency; communication security requires separate work.

Our contribution is an executable connection between human-authored instructions and the evidence available when those instructions arrive.

BioTwin makes that connection visible: which evidence was reviewed, what changed, why a branch applies, and when the software cannot make a supported selection.

The intended benefit is greater crew autonomy within human-defined instructions, with potential relevance to polar stations and other remote settings. Clinical benefit, usability with unfamiliar users and flight qualification remain future validation work.
